candidates: Shell scripts that use bash-specific features (e.g. in scripts/) should start with `set -euxo pipefail` immediately after the shebang. `-e` exits on any command failure, `-u` exits on references to unset variables, `-o pipefail` propagates failures through pipes, and `-x` prints each command before execution to aid CI/CD debugging. This removes the need for per-command `|| exit` guards.

Use the `.bash` file extension (not `.sh`) for scripts that require bash-specific syntax or rely on bash being the interpreter. The `.sh` extension implies POSIX shell compatibility and may cause the script to be invoked under `sh`/`dash` (e.g. via `sh ./script.sh` or as a source'd file), bypassing the bash shebang and breaking bash-only constructs.

Do not use bare `|| exit` (without an explicit exit code) in shell scripts. `|| exit` with no argument exits with status 0 (success), masking the real failure code and misleading callers or CI pipelines that check exit status. Use `|| exit $?` to propagate the actual failure, or—better—use `set -e` at the top of the script so all errors are automatically propagated without per-command guards.
